entry.title: 5 Things Nobody Tells You About Riding in Amsterdam
entry.excerpt: Tram tracks, two locks and the art of the bell — the unwritten rules we wish someone had told us on day one.

children.text: I moved to Amsterdam with a bike, a map and a great deal of confidence. Two of those three lasted about a week. Nobody hands you a rulebook when you arrive, partly because most of the rules are not written down anywhere. You learn them the hard way, usually in front of an audience. So here, from someone who has made most of these mistakes personally, are five things we wish someone had told us on day one.
1. Cross tram tracks at an angle, never parallel

Tram rails have a groove almost exactly the width of a bicycle tyre, which stops feeling like a coincidence the first time your front wheel drops into one. If that happens while you are riding alongside the rail, the wheel stops steering and you stop being upright. It is fast, it is undignified, and it happens to locals too.

The fix is simple. Whenever you need to cross tracks, do it as close to a right angle as you can manage: check behind you, swing out a little, then cut across decisively. Be twice as careful when it has been raining, because wet steel has roughly the grip of a bar of soap.
2. Two locks, one to something fixed

Amsterdam famously has more bikes than people, and a lively trade in bikes that used to belong to someone else. The city fishes thousands out of the canals every year, and not all of them fell in by accident.

The local setup is two locks. The first is the frame lock, the ring bolted to the back of most city bikes, which stops anyone simply riding off. The second is a heavy chain or D-lock that goes through the frame and around something that cannot move: a rack, a railing, a lamppost. Not another bike. Not a flimsy sign. Something fixed.

It feels like overkill until the morning you find a single front wheel still locked to the rack, the rest of your bike having left without you. Good locks cost a lot less than a new bike. Use both, every time, even when you are
only popping in for a minute
3. The bell is a conversation, not an insult

Visitors often flinch at a bell behind them, as if they have just been sworn at. They have not. Here the bell is punctuation. One quick ring means "I'm here, just so you know." Two means "coming past." A long, insistent ring usually means someone is standing in the bike lane photographing a canal, and might like to step onto the pavement.

Use yours freely and without guilt. A friendly ding as you approach a group, a drifting pedestrian or a wobbly rider saves everyone a fright. When someone rings at you, don't take it personally; hold your line and let them by. That's the whole conversation. And if your bike doesn't have a bell, get one. In the Netherlands it is the law.
4. Signal with your hands, and never stop suddenly

The bike lanes here run on a kind of unspoken choreography: hundreds of people moving at slightly different speeds, all trusting that nobody will do anything unexpected. The quickest way to break that trust is to stop dead, perhaps because you spotted a nice café or finally worked out where you are on your phone.

Before you turn, stick your arm out in the direction you are going, early enough for it to mean something. Before you stop, glance over your shoulder, drift to the right-hand edge of the path and only then brake. Never just halt in the middle of the lane. The person behind you is closer than you think, and is almost certainly holding a coffee.
5. The free ferries behind Centraal are part of the network

Walk through Centraal station to the water side and you will find the free ferries across the IJ, shuttling people and bikes to Amsterdam Noord from early morning until late at night. They are not a tourist attraction. They are part of the road. Commuters roll on, stand with their bikes, check their phones and roll off the other side a few minutes later without a second thought.
Use them. They are the quickest way to NDSM, the parks of Noord and the whole of Waterland beyond, where several of our
favourite day trips
begin. Let people off first, walk your bike on and off, and resist the urge to ride down the ramp the moment the gate opens.

None of this is complicated, and within a couple of weeks it all becomes second nature. You will cross tracks without thinking, ring your bell with a flourish and roll onto the ferry like you have done it all your life. Then one day a visitor will stop dead in front of you in the bike lane, and you will ring, smile, and remember that you were that person once. We all were.
